clothing-line.teach: Every methodology question on either paper has the same three moves, whatever the scenario: identify an approach, justify it against the words in front of you, outline what the work would look like. Nothing else earns marks.
clothing-line.ask: This assignment says the requirements MAY NOT be clearly stated at the beginning. What does that one clause rule out?

clothing-line.check: Every predictive method, because a predictive approach fixes requirements upfront.
clothing-line.teach: Methods split into two families, and the exam wants the split by name. Predictive: requirements defined upfront, a linear sequence, heavy documentation, limited flexibility for change. Adaptive: requirements evolve, iterative and incremental, strong user involvement, working software over documentation.
clothing-line.ask: So which family, and name two methods inside it?

clothing-line.check: Adaptive: Agile, and either RAD or system prototyping.
clothing-line.teach: Now the six selection criteria, which is the single most examined table in Module One: clarity of user requirements, familiarity with technology, system complexity, system reliability, short time schedules, schedule visibility. Unclear requirements point at prototyping; unfamiliar technology at throwaway prototyping; a short schedule at RAD.
clothing-line.ask: You have named Agile. Out of the marks for this part, how much is the naming worth?

clothing-line.check: Almost none. The marks are in the justification.
clothing-line.teach: So justify by quoting the scenario back, clause by clause, and answering each clause with a feature: requirements not clear at the start, answered by requirements that evolve iteration by iteration; a client who will want changes, answered by each iteration ending in a working increment and a review.
clothing-line.ask: Part 5 asks whether you refuse or agree to late features. Is there a right answer?

clothing-line.check: No, but there is a right SHAPE: take a position, then give three reasons tied to the project.
clothing-line.teach: The examiner is testing judgement, not obedience. A strong answer agrees to add them into a later iteration or release rather than the current one, which is the incremental model's own rule: further analysis is allowed for LATER increments, but changes to the CURRENT one are not accepted. That is what keeps an increment finishable.
clothing-line.ask: And one habit is left, worth the last mark on any methodology answer anywhere. What have you not done?

clothing-line.check: Named the alternative you rejected, and why.
clothing-line.teach: Close with two lines: "Waterfall was rejected: it requires requirements to be clear and stable throughout, it is difficult to respond to change, and the customer sees nothing until it may be too late." That sentence is the difference between a pass and a good mark, and it costs ten seconds.

2425-q2.teach: This question wants the life cycle as a table in your head: for each phase, its objective, its activities, its deliverables. Write it that way in the hall and the marks are countable.
2425-q2.ask: Name the five phases of the SDLC in order, before the answer names four of them.

2425-q2.teach: Note what the question did: it named a four phased cycle, analysis, design, implementation and support, leaving Planning out. Answer the question as asked, and add one line saying the text also treats Planning as a phase. Never correct the examiner silently, and never ignore his wording.

2425-q2.check: Identify the scope, ensure the project is feasible, and produce a schedule, resource plan and budget.
2425-q2.teach: Its five activities: define the problem, produce the schedule, confirm feasibility, staff the project, launch the project. Feasibility is confirmed in Planning, in five kinds: economic, organisational, technical, resource, schedule. That trap is asked constantly.
2425-q2.ask: Analysis is next. What one word does the text use for what Analysis is?

2425-q2.teach: Analysis establishes WHAT the system must do, never HOW. Six activities: gather information, define requirements, prioritise requirements, build a prototype for discovery, generate and evaluate alternatives, review recommendations with management. Design then answers HOW, in five activities: application architecture, network, user and system interfaces, database, system controls.
2425-q2.ask: Implementation includes the changeover. What are the four ways to switch over?

2425-q2.check: Direct cutover, parallel, phased and pilot.
2425-q2.teach: Phased splits the SYSTEM, pilot splits the USERS: that pair is confused constantly. Support is the last phase, and its three activities are maintain, enhance and support the users through a help desk.
2425-q2.ask: Part (b) asks for three stakeholders and how each views a system. Who are they?

2425-q2.check: Users, management and technical staff, in the text's terms.
2425-q2.teach: The point is that each sees a different system: the user sees the work it helps them do, management sees a capital investment to be justified against costs and risks, and the technical staff see something to be built, integrated and maintained. Part (c) is the tools against techniques pair: tools are software products, techniques are strategies for completing an activity.

2526-q3.teach: Six parts, all Module One, all list questions. The technique for the whole question is the same: name the list, then tie one clause of it to the scenario. The Boys are automating a food business in Nigeria, so every answer can name food, orders or the shop.
2526-q3.ask: Part (a) asks the three questions feasibility analysis answers. What do you think they are?

2526-q3.check: Is it worth doing, can it be done, and can it be done in the time and with what we have.
2526-q3.teach: In the text's own terms: economic, do the benefits outweigh the costs; technical, are the technology and skills available; and organisational or operational, will the business accept and use it. The text also lists resource and schedule feasibility, so name five if the marks allow.
2526-q3.ask: Part (b): the first step of the analyst's approach is research and understand the problem. Name the other seven.

2526-q3.check: Verify the benefits outweigh the costs, define the requirements, develop alternatives, decide and recommend, define the details, implement, monitor.
2526-q3.teach: Eight in all, and the question asks for six more, so the two extra you have are insurance against one you cannot remember. Step 1 has three named parts the examiner asks for by name: who is involved, what business processes come into play, and what other systems would be affected.
2526-q3.ask: Part (c) asks how to explain to stakeholders what a model is. What IS a model, in the text's words?

2526-q3.check: A representation of an important aspect of the real world.
2526-q3.teach: So explain it by naming the aspect it leaves out: a DFD models what the system does with data and says nothing about screens; an ERD models the nouns and nothing about order. Use an analogy they already trust, a floor plan of their shop, and say that a model is cheap to change while a built system is not.
2526-q3.ask: Part (d) says the most important skill is people knowledge. Name the other two kinds, and pick one to explain.

2526-q3.teach: Technical: computers and how they work, storage, input and output, networks and protocols, programming languages and operating systems, and collaboration technology. Business: what business functions organisations perform, how they are structured and managed, and about this company in particular, what it does and what makes it successful. Either earns the marks if you give the detail.
2526-q3.ask: Part (e): the support group's three activities?

2526-q3.check: Maintain the system, enhance it, and support the users.
2526-q3.teach: Maintenance is fixing bugs and small adjustments; enhancement is the bigger changes from new regulations, the market or new infrastructure; support is the help desk, staff available for any technical or processing problem. Part (f), the analyst's other job roles, comes from the seven responsibilities: requirements analyst, system evaluator, feasibility assessor, modeller and documenter, liaison, solution recommender, implementation support.

restaurant-car.teach: The ERD from a narrative is the most asked question in Module Two, and it is a five step procedure. Step one: underline every noun the organisation keeps data about. Each becomes a rectangle, named with a SINGULAR noun.
restaurant-car.ask: In the restaurant, which nouns are entities, and which noun is not?

restaurant-car.check: Customer, Order and Menu Item are entities. The restaurant itself is not, because the system keeps no data about it.
restaurant-car.teach: An entity always has more than one instance: one named customer is not an entity, Customer is. Step two: attributes. Give each entity three or four, and mark the identifier, the attribute that picks out one instance and which should never be blank and never need to change.
restaurant-car.ask: Step three names the relationships. What part of speech names a relationship, and what shape carries it in this course text?

restaurant-car.check: An active verb, in a diamond, because this text uses Chen notation.
restaurant-car.teach: Customer Places Order. Order Contains Menu Item. Written that way the diagram reads as a sentence, which is also how you answer the read-it-back questions.
restaurant-car.ask: Step four is cardinality. Ask each relationship in BOTH directions. Can one order contain many items, and can one item appear on many orders?

restaurant-car.check: Yes and yes, so it is many to many.
restaurant-car.teach: Yes and yes is M:N, and a many to many is resolved with an associative entity when the model is built. In the car rental question the examiner says it outright, "including any associative entity needed to record each individual rental": that sentence is telling you a many to many is hiding in the scenario.
restaurant-car.ask: Why can the rental not simply be an attribute of Customer or of Vehicle?

restaurant-car.check: Because the dates and the cost belong to the PAIRING, not to either one alone.
restaurant-car.teach: Introducing Rental turns one many to many into two one to many relationships, which is what makes the model buildable. Step five, and the part most answers drop: ordinality. Cardinality is the maximum, ordinality the minimum, optional at zero or mandatory at one.
restaurant-car.ask: A vehicle sits on the forecourt never yet rented. Mandatory or optional, and on which side?

restaurant-car.check: Optional, on the Vehicle side of the relationship to Rental.
restaurant-car.teach: And a Rental must have both a customer and a vehicle, so those sides are mandatory. Say both for every line, name your notation, and if the paper asks for Information Engineering or crow's foot instead, draw the fork on the many end and keep the same reasoning.

2425-q3.teach: A DFD answers one question: what does the system DO with data. Four symbols carry the whole notation, and the naming rules are marks on their own.
2425-q3.ask: Name the four elements and the shape of each, before the answer does.

2425-q3.check: External agent, a rectangle. Data flow, an arrow. Process, a rounded rectangle. Data store, an open ended rectangle.
2425-q3.teach: Naming: an agent is a singular noun, a flow is named with nouns, a process must be a verb and must not be procedural, and a data store takes a noun with no verbs. The text's own bad example is "Add 1 to the counter", which should be "Increment counter".
2425-q3.ask: In this warehouse, the truck driver, the manager, the labourer and the storekeeper are all named. Which of them are external agents?

2425-q3.check: The truck driver. The manager, labourer and storekeeper work inside the system, so their work is the processes.
2425-q3.teach: That judgement decides whether your diagram is clean or crowded. Anyone whose work the system records is INSIDE it; anyone who hands something in or takes something out is outside. Reports going to the manager are then flows from a process to an agent only if he is treated as a recipient, and the question says the report is disseminated to him, so he is.
2425-q3.ask: Now the levels. What is on a context diagram that is not on a Level 0, and the other way round?

2425-q3.check: Context has the whole system as one process and usually no data stores. Level 0 has the major processes AND the stores.
2425-q3.teach: And there is exactly one Level 0 per system, which is asked directly. A Level 1 explodes ONE process from Level 0, never the whole diagram.
2425-q3.ask: Part (e) asks for three ways to validate your diagrams. One of them is the single most examined DFD rule. Which?

2425-q3.check: Balancing: the inputs and outputs of a process are conserved when it is decomposed.
2425-q3.teach: The other two: check every process for the three errors, black hole with no outputs, miracle with no inputs, gray hole whose inputs cannot produce its outputs; and check every flow touches a process, which rules out store to store, agent to agent and store to agent.
2425-q3.ask: Part (b) asks how a data store should be named. What is the rule, and what is the phrase that separates a store from a flow?

2425-q3.check: A noun, avoiding verbs and physical descriptions. A store is data at rest; a flow is data in motion.
2425-q3.teach: Write that sentence into the answer: it is one line and it proves you know the difference the examiner is testing. Then, for part (d), draw the ERD first and the Level 0 second: the nouns you find for the ERD are the stores you will need for the DFD, so the two halves feed each other.

2526-q1.teach: This question is the heaviest drawing question on either paper: an ERD, three DFD levels, a list question and a read-it-back. Take them in the order printed, and keep the same entity names throughout so the examiner can follow you.
2526-q1.ask: In the narrative, who or what are the entities? Watch the trap in the word supervisor.

2526-q1.check: Landlord, House, Agent, Supervisor, and Payment or Rent.
2526-q1.teach: The supervisor is the TENANT in this story, which the wording hides. Read the whole narrative once before naming anything: the relationships, owns, manages, rents, pays, forwards, are the verbs your diamonds will carry.
2526-q1.ask: The landlord owns one of many houses, and the agent manages many houses. What cardinalities does that give you?

2526-q1.check: Landlord owns houses, one to many. Agent manages houses, one to many.
2526-q1.teach: Quote the phrase beside each one: "owns one of many houses", "who manages many houses". A cardinality justified by the examiner's own words cannot be argued with.
2526-q1.ask: Now part (b), three diagrams. What sits on the context diagram for this system?

2526-q1.check: One process, the whole lettings system, with the Landlord, the Agent and the Supervisor around it.
2526-q1.teach: Then Level 0: the major processes, numbered, with the stores, and there is exactly one of these. Then Level 1, exploding the rent payment process only, which is what part (b)(iii) names.
2526-q1.ask: Before you hand it in, what one sentence do you write under the Level 1 diagram?

2526-q1.check: That the diagrams balance: the flows in and out of the parent are all accounted for among the children.
2526-q1.teach: Ten seconds, one mark, every time. Part (c) then leaves diagrams behind: three more reasons a project succeeds and three why it fails. Answer from the text's nine principles, which is the nearest thing it has to a list of success factors: user involvement, a problem solving approach, phases and activities, standards, justification as a capital investment, willingness to cancel or revise scope, divide and conquer, design for growth and change, and proper planning and project management.
2526-q1.ask: Part (d) prints a small diagram and asks you to read it forwards and backwards. What does reading it backwards mean?

2526-q1.check: Stating the same relationship from the other entity's point of view.
2526-q1.teach: "One Customer places many Orders" forwards, "each Order is placed by exactly one Customer" backwards. Read every line of a given ERD both ways and you have answered any read-it-back question, in this paper and in 2024/2025 Q3(c) and Q4(b).

2425-q1.teach: Requirements questions have a house style, and it is the same on both papers: name the technique, then say who you would use it on, what it collects, why it suits this project, and one limitation. Four short clauses each.
2425-q1.ask: Name the seven fact finding techniques before the answer lists them.

2425-q1.check: Sampling documentation, research and site visits, observation, questionnaires, interviews, prototyping, and joint requirements planning.
2425-q1.teach: For a library system, the cheapest information is already written down: sampling the existing documentation, the accession registers, the loan slips and the overdue reports, which shows the real business rules and the data quality problems without costing a librarian a minute.
2425-q1.ask: Which technique would you pair with it, given you must reach students, librarians and management?

2425-q1.check: Questionnaires for the many, interviews for the few.
2425-q1.teach: Questionnaires collect from many respondents quickly and cheaply, in two formats: free format, where the respondent writes, and fixed format, where they choose, in multiple choice, rating or ranking. Interviews are the expensive one, so reserve them and prepare an interview guide.
2425-q1.ask: Part (b) wants functional and non functional requirements. What separates the two?

2425-q1.check: Functional says what the system must DO; non functional says how well it must do it.
2425-q1.teach: Functional for a library: issue a loan, reserve a title, calculate a fine, produce an overdue list. Non functional: respond within two seconds, be available during opening hours, keep borrower data private, run on the existing hardware. Write them as numbered one liners, never as a paragraph.
2425-q1.ask: 2025/2026 Q5 adds three more categories: business, user and system requirements. What is the difference between a business requirement and a functional one?

2425-q1.check: A business requirement is the outcome the organisation wants; a functional requirement is a thing the system does to deliver it.
2425-q1.teach: So: business, cut the time to find a title; user, a student can search the catalogue from a phone; functional, the system searches by title, author and subject; non functional, results in under two seconds; system, it runs on the existing web server and integrates with the student register. One line each, five labels, five marks.
2425-q1.ask: Part (b)(iii) asks why elicitation should involve users from different organisational levels. One sentence?

2425-q1.check: Because each level sees a different system, so asking only one level produces requirements that are incomplete or contradictory.
2425-q1.teach: Management sees cost and control, supervisors see the workflow, clerks see the screen they use all day. The text's own reason is that people are the source of requirements information, and conflicting requirements have to be found and resolved before they are built.

sports-centre.teach: A use case diagram is four steps, and the course text numbers them, which means the examiner marks them: actors, use cases, association lines, then include and extend. Write the four as headings and answer under each.
sports-centre.ask: Step one. Who are the actors here, and what rule names them?

sports-centre.check: The Customer and the Staff or Admin, named with nouns.
sports-centre.teach: The five questions that find actors: who provides input, who receives output, are interfaces required for other systems, are there events triggered automatically at a set time, and who maintains information in the system. Question three is the one that earns the extra mark here.
sports-centre.ask: Payment is taken and a notification is sent. What does that make the payment company?

sports-centre.check: An actor: an external server actor, because it responds to a request from the use case.
sports-centre.teach: Four types, and the exam asks you to tell them apart: primary business actor benefits, primary system actor touches the keyboard, external server actor responds to a request, external receiver actor receives output without being primary.
sports-centre.ask: Step two: what makes a phrase in the narrative a use case?

sports-centre.check: It is something an actor DOES, written as a verb phrase.
sports-centre.teach: Create Account, Log In, Check Availability, Make Booking, Make Payment, Cancel Booking, Add Facility, Generate Reports. Every one goes in an oval inside a boundary rectangle, and the actors stand outside it. An undrawn boundary loses marks on its own.
sports-centre.ask: Two of those happen on every single booking. Which, and what relationship is that?

sports-centre.check: Check Availability and Make Payment, and that is include.
sports-centre.teach: Include is always, extend is sometimes. Both are dashed arrows, so the label and the direction are all you have, and the extend arrow points FROM the extension TO the base: "Cancel Booking extends Make Booking". Say it aloud and the arrow follows the sentence.
sports-centre.ask: The second half asks for a narrative. Name as many of its seven parts as you can.

sports-centre.check: Name and identifier, actors, description and goal, preconditions, main flow, alternative flows, postconditions.
sports-centre.teach: The part that separates a full answer is alternative flows, the failures: no slot free, payment declined, the slot taken while paying. The text praises use cases precisely because they surface exceptions and error handling, so writing three failure lines is writing the reason the technique exists.

2526-q4.teach: You are not preparing this question, so four frames only, for the fallback case. Every part of it belongs to the design and acquisition material, and the shape of each answer is a short list tied to the scenario.
2526-q4.ask: The scenario says the time frame is short and the project skills are not strategic. What does that combination point at?

2526-q4.check: Buying a package rather than building it, or outsourcing.
2526-q4.teach: That is the whole of part (a): a short schedule and skills that are not core to the business point at purchasing a packaged solution, with customisation. Supporting factors: the requirements are common to the industry, the cost and timeline are predictable, and the vendor carries the maintenance.
2526-q4.ask: Part (d) asks for three principles of interface design. Guess any two.

2526-q4.check: Consistency, and clear feedback to the user.
2526-q4.teach: The usual list: layout consistency, content awareness so the user always knows where they are, aesthetics, user experience matched to who the users are, consistency across screens, and minimal user effort, no more than three clicks to anything.
2526-q4.ask: Part (e) asks you to design and populate a relational database. What earns the marks, beyond the table itself?

2526-q4.check: The primary keys, and the foreign key that joins the tables.
2526-q4.teach: Three tables, Customer, Order and Payment Type, each with at least three columns and five rows of plausible dummy data, every identifier marked as the primary key, and Order carrying the customer and payment type ids as foreign keys. Draw it as three small tables, not as prose.
